s0.p3: A little ahead of time, let us introduce the concept of a **global object**.
s0.p4: A **global object** is the environment in which we "live" (operate) and beyond which we cannot go.
s0.p6:
On the client side JS works in the browser, in the console of which, by the way, we perform all the operations below.

This is possible because the **V8** engine built into each browser interprets our code and executes it.
s0.p8: Simplistically speaking, the **global object** for us is the browser (more precisely, its **object model**, but we will deal with that later).
s0.p9: The browser itself works in the operating system and has access to its capabilities.
s0.p10: But we cannot go outside the browser and interact with the operating system directly.
s0.p11: So, the operating system allocates system resources, in particular memory, for the work of applications, including the browser.
s0.p12: The browser manages the memory resource allocated to it, part of which it allocates to the **V8** engine.
s0.p13: Next we will talk about variables, i.e. the memory that will be used by our application.
s0.p14: For our code, access to the global object is provided by the **⟦f0⟧** variable.
s0.p16: Memory is a huge number of cells, each of which can contain 0 or 1.
s0.p18:
Such a cell is a **bit** of memory.
That is why the binary number system was the basis for the first computers.
The **8 bits** make **1 byte** of memory.
s0.p20: A maximum of 8 units can be placed in **1 byte** of memory, i.e. the binary number 11111111.
s0.p21: In decimal notation this would be the number 255 without a sign.
s0.p22: If **byte** (8 bits) is interpreted as a signed number, one bit will contain the sign of the number (**+ **or** -**), so the maximum number with a sign that can ‘fit’ into one byte is 127 (seven units).

s0.p28: As you have already guessed, the computer can only work with binary numbers, i.e. sets of zeros and ones.
s0.p29: The reasonable question is how does the computer store text, pictures and videos, etc.

s0.p31: Any character is represented by its code (number):
s0.p32: Thus, any information is represented in computer memory by sets of zeros and ones, and managing memory allocation is a very complex process.
s0.p33: It is quite improbable to operate on physical memory addresses to access data.
s0.p35: You don't need to know the physical addresses where your data will be stored.
s0.p36: You need to come up with a name for each data item, and tell the engine what data item you will store under that name.
s0.p37: This is how a **variable** is created.
s0.p38: So, **variables** make it easier for you to manipulate your data and keep your operating system and running applications safe.
s0.p40: As you have already realised, any data is stored in computer memory as a set of zeros and ones.
s0.p41: In order for the engine to correctly interpret this set of zeros and ones, it must know what was stored at the given address: a number, a string or something else.

s0.p49: ^^Variables can store numbers, strings, logical values, specific **⟦f1⟧** and **⟦f2⟧** values, as well as **reference type** data, which we'll get to later.^^
s0.p50: So, it is important that the engine knows the type of the data that is stored in the variable.
s0.p51: Unlike languages with strict typing, we do not need to specify the type of data we intend to store in a variable when declaring it.
s0.p52: **The data type is determined during the process of assigning a value.**
